title: A man up a tree
hook: a man hangs from a branch by his teeth; someone asks why Bodhidharma came west (Gateless Gate 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dogen's blue mountains, walking. Your line: the mountains walk. Did a hill, a building, anything that looked still, seem to move for you? Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

A man is up a tree. Not resting on a branch, not holding on with his hands. He's hanging from a branch by his teeth. His hands grip nothing. His feet touch nothing. Below him is a long drop. And just then, someone standing under the tree calls up a question: why did Bodhidharma come from the west? It's a question Zen stories use to ask what this whole tradition is about. If the man keeps quiet, he fails the person asking. If he opens his mouth to answer, he falls. That's the whole story. It's case five of a collection called the Gateless Gate, and it ends with a question for you: what would you do?
screen: `HANGING BY HIS TEETH.` → `A QUESTION FROM BELOW.` → `SPEAK AND FALL. STAY SILENT AND FAIL.`

segments.voice: First, who tells it. The case is credited to a teacher named Xiangyan, called Kyogen in Japanese. He sets up the scene, and then he stops. He doesn't say what the man did. The koan hands the problem to whoever is listening. Second, the trap. Both choices look like losing. Answer, and you fall. Don't answer, and you've turned away someone who asked you the biggest thing they could ask. The mind tries to find a third door: shout, nod, hum through your teeth. A clever escape misses the point. The koan isn't a riddle with a trick answer. It's built to leave thinking with nowhere to stand. Third, why a tree at all. The koans this week each carry some version of this pressure. Here the man has no hands free and no ground. That's a picture of a moment that can come to any life: a hospital hallway, a phone call, a choice where every road costs something. Zen students sit with the case, not to solve it like a puzzle, but to stay with the squeeze long enough to find out who is hanging there. Fourth, the comment. The compiler, Wumen, added a short comment and a verse to each case. In paraphrase, he says that even a flood of eloquence is no use here, and that if you can answer in this spot, you bring dead things back to life. He doesn't hand over the answer either. Some readers notice that the man is still alive at the end of the story. Nothing has fallen yet. The whole koan happens in one held breath, with the teeth still holding.
screen: `XIANGYAN SETS IT UP AND STOPS.` · `BOTH DOORS LOOK LIKE LOSING.` · `NO HANDS, NO GROUND.` · `WUMEN: ELOQUENCE IS NO USE.` · then, large: `HANGING BY THE TEETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one choice in your own life where every option seems to cost something. Don't solve it. Don't list pros and cons. Just hold it, the way the man holds the branch, and feel where the squeeze sits in the body: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Breathe into that spot. When the mind races for a third door, notice the racing, and come back to the breath and the held question. The bell holds the time.
A man up a tree. Xiangyan's koan, case five of the Gateless Gate: hanging by the teeth, asked the great question, with no safe way to speak or stay silent. Today's word.
screen: `A MAN UP A TREE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hanging by the teeth. Today, when a choice feels impossible, take one breath before you grab for an exit, and notice who is doing the hanging. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen, students are given koans such as this one to hold through sitting and daily life, and they present their response to the teacher in private interview rather than writing an answer down.

fork.setup: you're hanging from the branch by your teeth. someone below asks why Bodhidharma came from the west. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Xiangyan never says. the case ends with the question, and Zen students take it into sitting and into the teacher's room.

original.note: Chinese title of Gateless Gate case 5, 'Xiangyan up a tree'. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.

trapdoor: what you thought: a riddle with a clever answer.
what it means: a scene where every choice costs, given to students to hold until thinking has nowhere to stand.
what a scholar hears: case five of the Gateless Gate, credited to Xiangyan, with Wumen's comment that eloquence is no use here.

All Gateless Gate material paraphrased; no public-domain English translation was quoted. Check the case details: hanging by the teeth, hands holding no branch, feet on no support; the question 'why did Bodhidharma come from the west'; answering means falling, not answering means failing the questioner.
Wumen's comment paraphrased as 'even a flood of eloquence is no use' and 'if you can answer here, you bring dead things back to life'; confirm the paraphrase.
'A stock question in Zen' is stated without a count; confirm.
'Every koan in this week' refers to the week's planned koan days (1242–1247); 'some readers notice the man is still alive' is offered as a reading, not a teaching of the text.
Original-language title 香嚴上樹: confirm characters and pronunciation.
Editor pass: cut the general claim about how Zen teachers meet clever escapes; softened 'a stock question in Zen' to a description of what the question asks.
